documents.unit: Martha Bradley Evans Center for Teaching Excellence
documents.title: Fall 2023 Instructional Guidelines on generative AI
documents.stance_why: The document sets no AI rule for students itself; it 'recommends that all faculty include a statement' and offers 'suggested' practices and resources, leaving decisions to instructors, so it delegates.
documents.summary: Anne Cook, director of the Evans Center for Teaching Excellence, issues Fall 2023 instructional guidance with a suggested academic-honesty syllabus statement, assessment tips, notes on detectors, and learning resources for instructors.

units.why: The CTE 'recommends' every instructor add a syllabus statement saying misrepresenting AI content as one's own is misconduct, so it addresses instructors at course set-up; type P09 (statement in every syllabus) fits because the recommendation is about the syllabus, and the misconduct classification is coded in the next unit.
units.anchor: MBECTE recommends that all faculty include a statement on their syllabus
units.fit_note: The recommendation is non-binding ('recommends'), and the statement's content is that misrepresenting AI work is misconduct.

units.why: The suggested syllabus text classes use of generative AI 'without citation, documentation, or authorization' as academic dishonesty; this is a classification of improper AI use as misconduct (P36), and it also implies citation/authorization requirements but the main act is labelling it dishonesty.
units.anchor: This includes the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools without citation, documentation, or authorization.

units.why: The statement says students who commit dishonesty 'may be subject to academic sanctions' under the Student Code; it ties AI misconduct to existing sanctions without stating specific penalties, so P36 rather than P37.
units.anchor: may be subject to academic sanctions as per the University of Utah’s Student Code

units.why: For out-of-class work the CTE 'recommend[s]' assignments requiring more than an answer (reflect, analyze, critique, video or poster); this is assignment redesign around AI (P35), addressed to instructors.
units.anchor: we recommend using assignments that require students to do more than just produce an answer

units.why: Requiring citations or documentation 'difficult for an AI generator' is a further assignment-design strategy against AI, so P35 (redesign around AI).
units.anchor: Requiring students to include citations or documentation in a manner that would be difficult for

units.why: Instructors are told to 'Familiarize yourself with popular AI tools' and the responses they produce to assignment prompts; this is faculty learning advice before setting policy, P63.
units.anchor: Familiarize yourself with popular AI tools and the kinds of responses they may produce

units.why: The CTE says it recommended that faculty 'not rely on Turnitin's Originality score' because of reliability issues; this is a statement against relying on an AI detector, P39 (P69 would need an evidence-standard rule).
units.anchor: recommended that faculty not rely on Turnitin’s Originality score to detect all AI usage

units.why: Faculty are 'encouraged to explore independent AI detection tools' such as ZeroGPT; this encourages using detectors to identify misuse, so P40 (detection tools), noting it sits in tension with the Turnitin caution.
units.anchor: Faculty are encouraged to explore independent AI detection tools
units.fit_note: Encourages exploring tools rather than prescribing a use; no standard of evidence given.

units.why: Faculty are told to 'stay abreast' of AI developments in their field and given outlets to follow; a duty/encouragement to stay informed, P102.
units.anchor: we recommend faculty stay abreast of developments in their own field

units.why: The page lists CTE events and workshops on AI and writing and AI in the classroom; this is faculty support for learning about AI (P63), not a rule.
units.anchor: MBECTE will also hold a campuswide workshop on AI and Writing on November 30.

units.why: Level 3 points faculty to self-paced AI courses and a micro bootcamp; learning resources for instructors, so P63 (faculty-only, not P70).
units.anchor: Level up with self-paced courses on AI.

documents.title: Gen AI Acceptable Use - AI & You Student Guide
documents.stance_why: It offers tiers: 'Instructors will communicate the level of AI use permitted for each assignment' and the scale runs from Level 0 to Level 5, so the decision is delegated and the tiers are listed.
tiers: Level 3 AI for Specified Task Completion
Level 4 Full AI Use with Human Oversight
Level 5 Full AI Use without Human Oversight
documents.summary: The student guide sets a six-level scale of AI use (0 to 5) with disclosure standards and examples, and says instructors will announce the level per assignment. Undisclosed required use is academic misconduct under Policy 6-410, and an APA citation and disclosure template is provided.

units.why: The guide says 'Instructors will communicate the level of AI use permitted for each assignment'; the permission is set by the instructor per assignment, so P04 (let each instructor or assignment set the rule) rather than P05, which is the separate tier unit.
units.anchor: Instructors will communicate the level of AI use permitted for each assignment.

units.why: Instructors 'may set different AI use levels for different assignments within the same course'; per-assignment variation, P04.
units.anchor: Instructors may set different AI use levels for different assignments within the same course.

units.why: Defines which tools the scale covers ('ChatGPT EDU, Gemini, Copilot, image generators, and other AI tools that create new content'); a scope definition, P61.
units.anchor: This scale applies to tools such as ChatGPT EDU, Gemini, Copilot, image generators

units.why: Students are 'encouraged to use university-approved AI tools' for security and data protection under the enterprise agreement; use of institution-approved tools is P92.
units.anchor: Students are encouraged to use university-approved AI tools

units.why: Students with questions about permitted AI use should direct them to the instructor, mentor or adviser; ask-when-unsure, P10.
units.anchor: Questions about permitted AI use should be directed to the instructor, mentor, or adviser

units.why: 'Always check your specific course syllabus' makes students responsible for finding the rules per course; P78 fits better than P10 because it is not about asking when unsure.
units.anchor: Always check your specific course syllabus.

units.why: Beyond citing, students 'should be able to explain' how and why they used AI; an accountability-for-understanding rule, P30 though it concerns the AI process rather than every line (fit note).
units.anchor: you should be able to explain to your instructor/mentor/adviser how you used AI
units.fit_note: Asks students to explain how and why they used AI, not to explain every line of submitted work.

units.why: Level 0 is defined as work 'completed entirely on your own, without any AI assistance'; a named tier at the no-AI end (P05), with unit_stance prohibit.
units.anchor: The assignment is completed entirely on your own, without any AI assistance.

units.why: Level 0 examples are a handwritten in-class exam and a proctored closed-book exam 'with no devices allowed'; no-AI in-person assessment, P22.
units.anchor: proctored in person with no devices allowed

units.why: Level 1 lets students 'refine, debug, translate, and/or polish' their own content with AI; editing/polishing permission, P91 (the debug example is the unit after next).
units.anchor: You write the content yourself, then use AI to help refine, debug, translate, and/or polish

units.why: Level 1 says AI 'should not generate new content for you'; ban on AI producing the submitted content at this tier, P19.
units.anchor: should not generate new content for you

units.why: Level 1 example: AI suggests a bug fix to code that does not compile, and the student 'still verif[ies] on [their] own'; AI-assisted debugging, P13.
units.anchor: You ask AI to help suggest a bug fix.

units.why: Levels 1 and 2 state 'No disclosure, unless specified'; it sets a no-disclosure default at lower tiers, which is the nearest to P24 but reverses it (fit note).
units.anchor: No disclosure, unless specified.
units.fit_note: States that disclosure is NOT required at Levels 1-2 unless the instructor specifies it.

units.why: Level 2 makes AI a 'thought partner' to brainstorm and generate ideas while the content submitted is the student's own; brainstorming, P15.
units.anchor: use AI to help brainstorm, build outlines, search for tools, explain concepts,

units.why: The same Level 2 description lets AI 'explain concepts'; kept as a separate unit since concept explanation is a tutor-like use, P12.
units.anchor: AI is a thought partner
units.policy: At Level 2 AI may be used to explain concepts as a thought partner

units.why: Level 2 requires that 'the actual content you submit is your own'; students own what they submit, P29.
units.anchor: but the actual content you submit is your own

units.why: Level 2 example allows an international student to translate their own work into English with AI; translation is prose-specific, P18.
units.anchor: uses generative AI to translate work from their native language into English

units.why: Level 3 allows AI-generated content 'used verbatim or lightly edited'; generation under conditions (critical review, citation), P16.
units.anchor: You use AI to complete and generate content that may be used verbatim or lightly

units.why: Level 3 requires the student to 'think critically' and 'take responsibility for reviewing and evaluating all AI-generated content'; verification duty, P31.
units.anchor: take responsibility for reviewing and evaluating all AI-generated content

units.why: Level 3 requires APA in-text citation and reference entry for AI content; P25 chosen over P24 because it specifies the format of the citation.
units.anchor: AI-created content must be cited using proper APA style.

units.why: Levels 3 and 4 add that 'links to AI chat(s) may be submitted' depending on instructor; submission of transcripts, P26.
units.anchor: links to AI chat(s) may be submitted with the submission

units.why: The Level 3 CS example has a student use an AI coding assistant to 'generate or autocomplete a small function' while completing design and testing the system; limited AI-generated code, P16.
units.anchor: use an AI coding assistant to generate or autocomplete a small function

units.why: Level 4 lets students use AI 'freely throughout the assignment as a co-pilot'; permissive tier, P02.
units.anchor: A student uses AI freely throughout the assignment as a co-pilot to support their work.

units.why: Level 4 'key responsibility is the human review of everything AI produces' and the product must reflect the student's judgment; P29 chosen over P31 since it centers on the final product reflecting own judgment.
units.anchor: making sure the final product reflects your own judgment and understanding

units.why: Level 4 requires citing 'all uses of AI using APA style, including in-text citations and reference entries'; P24 disclosure (the format is covered by the Level 3 unit).
units.anchor: You must cite all uses of AI using APA style

units.why: A Level 4 example has an engineering student use an advanced coding agent to generate software for a complex project; allowed use of coding agents, P07.
units.anchor: uses an advanced coding agent, such as ChatGPT Codex, to generate software for a complex
units.fit_note: Covers allowing an autonomous coding agent at Level 4 rather than restricting it.

units.why: Level 4 examples include 'submitting an AI use log and critical reflection'; documentation of process, P26.
units.anchor: combined with submitting an AI use log and critical reflection

units.why: Level 5 describes students who 'fully delegate academic judgment, grading decisions, research authorship' to AI without review; this defines an unacceptable use, P36.
units.anchor: Students fully delegate academic judgment, grading decisions, research authorship, or evaluative responsibilities to AI
units.fit_note: Defines the unacceptable use (full delegation) rather than stating the classification; the next unit states misconduct.

units.why: Level 5 says failing to disclose required AI use or delegating judgment 'may constitute academic misconduct and/or research misconduct'; misconduct classification, P36.
units.anchor: may constitute academic misconduct and/or research misconduct

units.why: The Level 5 example 'Generating code using a generative AI tool for an assignment that states that this assignment shall not use AI' bans generated code where the assignment says no AI; P19.
units.anchor: Generating code using a generative AI tool for an assignment that states that this assignment

units.why: Level 5 includes 'Posting AI-generated discussion posts in Canvas without review or disclosure'; example of misuse of unreviewed output, P31.
units.anchor: Posting AI-generated discussion posts in Canvas without review or disclosure.
units.fit_note: Combines no review and no disclosure; verification is the nearest fit.

units.why: 'If you use AI and do not disclose it when required, it is considered Academic Misconduct'; the nondisclosure itself is the violation, so P28 chosen over P36 because the rule is about disclosure.
units.anchor: If you use AI and do not disclose it when required, it is considered Academic

units.why: 'Whenever AI plays a meaningful role in your work, you should disclose and cite it'; a disclosure expectation, P24.
units.anchor: Whenever AI plays a meaningful role in your work, you should disclose and cite it.

units.why: The disclosure template asks for tool name, model/version and date and the purpose; specific details of the AI used, P25.
units.anchor: This assignment used generative AI (tool name, model/version, date)

units.why: The statement template says 'All outputs were reviewed, verified, and revised by the author'; models the verification and ownership claim, P31.
units.anchor: All outputs were reviewed, verified, and revised by the author.

units.why: The guide gives an APA reference format for AI tools as 'a baseline'; the citation details (author, name, version, URL), P25.
units.anchor: Here is the APA format the University of Utah recommends as a baseline.

documents.title: AI Tools for Education
documents.stance_why: The page tells instructors to set their own rules ('instructors should clearly state if, when, and how generative AI may be used') and gives no default for students, so it delegates.
documents.summary: The CTE's AI-for-teaching page advises instructors on syllabus statements, disclosure, privacy, assignment design, grading, and in-class activities, and describes campus AI tools. Most items are recommendations; the grading and data rules are stated as requirements.

units.why: The page states the CTE favors AI use 'Rather than banning or ignoring AI', designing learning that leverages its strengths; a pro-use stance addressed to instructors, P02.
units.anchor: Rather than banning or ignoring AI, educators can design learning experiences that leverage its strengths

units.why: Cites that '73% of employers use GenAI' and 55% of graduates were not prepared; a career-readiness rationale for teaching AI, P44.
units.anchor: 73% of employers use GenAI while more than half (55%) of graduates said their program

units.why: Faculty are urged 'moving beyond awareness to active engagement with AI tools in order to prepare students for a workforce that already demands AI literacy'; P44.
units.anchor: prepare students for a workforce that already demands AI literacy

units.why: States AI 'power[s] adaptive learning systems that tailor instruction to individual student needs'; a benefit statement, P87.
units.anchor: AI technologies power adaptive learning systems that tailor instruction to individual student needs

units.why: Names 'data privacy, algorithmic bias, intellectual property rights, and the potential commercialization of education' as ethical challenges; P53.
units.anchor: Ethical challenges—such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, intellectual property rights

units.why: CTE says it is 'committed to supporting instructors' with competencies and strategies for AI; faculty support, P63.
units.anchor: We are committed to supporting instructors in developing the digital competencies

units.why: Tip 1: 'Begin your course with an open discussion about AI'; explaining and discussing AI with students, P66.
units.anchor: Begin your course with an open discussion about AI.

units.why: Tip 1 asks instructors to clarify that tools 'can support—but not replace—student learning'; AI must not replace thinking, P32.
units.anchor: Clarify how tools like Microsoft Copilot can support—but not replace—student learning.

units.why: Tip 1 frames AI 'as a professional skill and ethical responsibility'; P44.
units.anchor: Frame AI as a professional skill and ethical responsibility.

units.why: Tip 2 urges assignments requiring 'analysis, synthesis, and evaluation—not just recall' and harder for AI to replicate; P35.
units.anchor: Use assignments that require analysis, synthesis, and evaluation—not just recall.

units.why: Instructors should 'Use the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS)' for assessment criteria; this points to a tiered scale, P05.
units.anchor: Use the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) to establish appropriate criteria for success for assessments.
units.fit_note: Recommends adopting an external scale rather than naming tiers itself.

units.why: Tip 3: 'Ask students to reflect on how they used AI in an assignment' with prompts and include it in the grade; reflection on AI use, P26.
units.anchor: Ask students to reflect on how they used AI in an assignment

units.why: Tip 4: 'giving students the option to complete assignments with or without AI tools' with AI-assisted and AI-free versions; an assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Consider giving students the option to complete assignments with or without AI tools.
units.fit_note: Also makes AI optional, which touches equity (P51).

units.why: Tip 5 'Ditch Detection Tools': detectors 'have repeatedly proven to be unreliable and inaccurate'; P39.
units.anchor: AI-detection tools have repeatedly proven to be unreliable and inaccurate

units.why: Detectors 'are not on the list of UIT-approved AI tools and could expose FERPA-secured data'; a data-protection reason, P50.
units.anchor: could expose FERPA-secured data to significant security risks

units.why: 'prevent misuse by designing clear, specific, and creative tasks—then emphasize honest communication and trust' offers prevention rather than detection; P99.
units.anchor: prevent misuse by designing clear, specific, and creative tasks

units.why: Instructors must 'Never enter or upload sensitive or restricted data' (PHI, FERPA, PII) into generative AI per Rule 4-004C; P50.
units.anchor: Never enter or upload sensitive or restricted data

units.why: 'Any intellectual property belonging to students, staff, or faculty should not be input without explicit consent'; input of others' IP, P52 with a fit note.
units.anchor: should not be input without explicit consent
units.fit_note: About consent for inputting others' IP, not ownership of outputs.

units.why: 'we highly recommend using Microsoft Copilot over other generative AI tools like ChatGPT' for data protection; preferring a vetted tool, P92.
units.anchor: we highly recommend using Microsoft Copilot over other generative AI tools like ChatGPT

units.why: 'using Microsoft Copilot for patient-related activity is prohibited'; a data-protection limit, P50.
units.anchor: using Microsoft Copilot for patient-related activity is prohibited

units.why: Copilot chat must not be used to share 'protected health information... and student information'; a restriction on data in the sanctioned tool, P50.
units.anchor: should never be shared through Microsoft Copilot chat

units.why: Instructors must verify the 'green shield' for every Copilot conversation; practical protection step, P50.
units.anchor: It is critical to verify that the green shield is present for all conversations.
units.fit_note: A procedural step for using the vetted tool rather than a data rule.

units.why: 'We highly recommend including a statement in your syllabus detailing expectations around use of generative AI tools'; P09.
units.anchor: We highly recommend including a statement in your syllabus

units.why: The sample statement treats generative AI use 'without citation, documentation, or authorization' as academic dishonesty; P36.
units.anchor: This includes the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools without citation, documentation, or authorization.

units.why: The sample statement says violators 'may be subject to academic sanctions as per Policy 6-410'; no specific penalty, P36.
units.anchor: may be subject to academic sanctions

units.why: 'You are free to use and edit the statement listed above' offers template language; P110.
units.anchor: You are free to use and edit the statement listed above.

units.why: 'Some departments may elect to create a broad AI policy for all courses in their department'; units setting rules, P85.
units.anchor: Some departments may elect to create a broad AI policy for all courses in their

units.why: 'instructors must proactively guide students by setting clear boundaries' since there is no universal standard; per-instructor rule-setting, P04.
units.anchor: instructors must proactively guide students by setting clear boundaries, explaining appropriate use, and adapting policies

units.why: 'instructors should clearly state if, when, and how generative AI may be used' in syllabus and assignment instructions; P09.
units.anchor: instructors should clearly state if, when, and how generative AI may be used

units.why: Gives acceptable examples ('brainstorming ideas, improving grammar, changing linguistic style'); P15 nearest, but includes grammar and style.
units.anchor: acceptable use cases (e.g. brainstorming ideas, improving grammar, changing linguistic style)

units.why: Gives a prohibited example: 'submitting AI-generated text as one's own work'; P19.
units.anchor: prohibited uses (e.g. submitting AI-generated text as one’s own work)

units.why: Notes there is 'no foolproof detection method for AI-generated content' and no standard for 'AI plagiarism'; limits on control, P82.
units.anchor: no foolproof detection method for AI-generated content

units.why: 'instructors might allow AI-generated support for researching a problem... but not for writing entire case analyses'; P19 for the ban on writing, with research use allowed.
units.anchor: allow AI-generated support for researching a problem and potential solutions but not for writing entire
units.fit_note: Also permits AI for researching a problem (P12/P104).

units.why: 'Here is an example policy that balances faculty independence with shared expectations'; sample policy, P110.
units.anchor: Here is an example policy that balances faculty independence with shared expectations.

units.why: 'Treat AI outputs like any other source that students must cite'; AI treated as a source under citation rules, P45 (not P96).
units.anchor: Treat AI outputs like any other source that students must cite.

units.why: Instructors should 'require them to openly acknowledge how they used it'; disclosure with each submission, P24.
units.anchor: require them to openly acknowledge how they used it

units.why: 'Prompts, any direct text or data from an AI model should be quoted or cited'; specifics of prompt and output, P25.
units.anchor: Prompts, any direct text or data from an AI model should be quoted or cited

units.anchor: should not be input into public AI tools

units.anchor: The same AI resources should be available to all students.

units.why: Students 'should understand that AI models can exhibit biases, make up information'; bias and harms, P53.
units.anchor: AI models can exhibit biases, make up information, or reflect limited perspectives

units.why: 'treat AI usage policies as living documents – solicit student feedback'; P54.
units.anchor: treat AI usage policies as living documents

units.why: 'instructors should take time to use and understand it themselves' before asking students to use a tool; P63.

units.why: Instructors should spend 'some class time to explaining how generative AI works'; AI literacy, P70.
units.anchor: Dedicating some class time to explaining

units.why: 'Creating a classroom culture where students can openly discuss their experiences with AI'; P66.
units.anchor: Creating a classroom culture where students can openly discuss their experiences with AI

units.why: 'Effective use of AI in coursework should always serve your learning objectives'; P83.
units.anchor: Effective use of AI in coursework should always serve your learning objectives

units.why: Example instruction: 'you must write the comparison analysis in your own words and explain the reasoning without AI assistance'; students stay the primary problem solver, P32.
units.anchor: you must write the comparison analysis in your own words and explain the reasoning without
units.fit_note: Also permits AI to research factual information.

units.why: 'instead of a basic essay question that an AI could easily answer' assign a context-rich project; P35.

units.why: An 'AI Usage Statement' asking which tool, for what purpose and how output was verified; P26 (reflection on AI use).
units.anchor: Students can be asked to reflect on how they used generative AI

units.why: 'Design rubrics and feedback to explicitly reward the analysis, creativity, and original thought'; P35.
units.anchor: Design rubrics and feedback to explicitly reward the analysis, creativity, and original thought

documents.title: Plagiarism & AI Policies
documents.stance_why: It states 'The allowed or disallowed use of AI in coursework will be at the discretion of the instructor', so the department sets no stance itself and delegates.
documents.summary: The ECE department's page says AI use in coursework is at the instructor's discretion and posted in the syllabus, research use rests with the supervisory chair, and publication follows journal rules. It quotes arXiv and IEEE guidance on responsibility and disclosure.

units.why: The department says it 'will also adhere' to new university, college or department AI policies; commits to following higher-level policy, P77.
units.anchor: ECE will also adhere to those policies

units.why: It notes that 'policies and practices related to AI are quickly evolving'; provisional policy, P54.
units.anchor: policies and practices related to AI are quickly evolving

units.why: Coursework AI use 'will be at the discretion of the instructor'; instructor sets the rule, P04.
units.anchor: The allowed or disallowed use of AI in coursework will be at the discretion of

units.anchor: should be posted in the course syllabus

units.why: Research AI use 'at the discretion of the student's supervisory committee chair'; research governance, P62.
units.anchor: The use of AI in research will be at the discretion of the student’s supervisory
